title: Noticing relevant problem features: activating prior knowledge affects problem solving by guiding encoding
extended_summary:
This paper asks whether activating learners’ prior arithmetic knowledge changes how they encode and solve mathematical equivalence problems such as 3 + 4 + 5 = 3 + __. The authors build on prior work showing that elementary and middle school students often struggle with these equations because their earlier arithmetic experiences lead them to treat the equal sign as an operator rather than a symbol of equivalence. The central question is not just whether prior knowledge hurts performance, but how it does so: by altering what features of the equation are noticed and encoded.

To test this, the study used a laboratory knowledge-activation paradigm with undergraduate students educated in the United States. Participants were randomly assigned to a knowledge-activation condition or a control condition. The activation tasks were designed to prime perceptual, conceptual, and procedural “operational patterns” associated with traditional arithmetic; control tasks used non-mathematical stimuli. Afterward, participants completed two objective tasks: briefly viewing equations and reconstructing them from memory to assess encoding, and separately solving equivalence problems.

The results showed that activating operational arithmetic knowledge reduced reconstruction accuracy, increased reconstruction of equations as if they were standard arithmetic problems, and decreased problem-solving accuracy. Participants in the activation condition were also more likely to use the add-all strategy, mirroring children’s typical errors. Mediation analyses indicated that inaccurate encoding partially explained the negative effect of activation on problem solving. The study concludes that prior arithmetic knowledge can hinder equivalence learning by guiding attention and encoding toward the wrong problem features, helping explain persistent difficulties with the equal sign and motivating instruction that highlights relational meanings rather than reinforcing arithmetic routines.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed experimental study with random assignment to knowledge activation vs. control, but it is not an RCT in an educational deployment sense and uses an adult laboratory sample rather than the target K-12 population. The design supports causal inference about mechanism, but external validity to classroom intervention contexts is limited.
impact_tier_rationale: The study shows a modest negative effect on a narrow mathematical task (equivalence problems), with effect sizes in the small-to-moderate range. It is informative for understanding why students struggle, but it does not test a scalable instructional intervention or demonstrate direct educational impact on K-12 learners.

finding.finding_summary: In this experiment with undergraduate students (n=115 for reconstruction; n=100 for problem solving), activating arithmetic operational knowledge reduced performance on mathematical equivalence problems. Participants in the knowledge-activation condition reconstructed fewer equations correctly (M=2.71 vs. 3.53; F(1,110)=11.96, p=0.001, ηp²=0.098) and solved fewer problems correctly (M=2.53 vs. 3.15; F(1,95)=6.25, p=0.014, ηp²=0.062) than controls.
finding.measure: Problem reconstruction accuracy and equivalence problem-solving accuracy
